questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: What is the typical resting membrane potential (RMP) of a large myelinated mammalian nerve fiber?
options: -70 to -90 mV (inside negative relative to outside)
+35 mV (inside positive relative to outside)
0 mV (electrically neutral across the membrane)
-10 mV (inside slightly negative)
questions.explain: Large myelinated nerve fibers typically have a resting membrane potential between -70 mV and -90 mV, with the intracellular compartment negative relative to the extracellular fluid.

open.q: State the typical resting membrane potential range (in mV) of a large mammalian nerve fiber.
accept: -70 to -90 mV
-70 mV to -90 mV
-70 mV

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: Which ion has the highest resting membrane permeability in typical neurons and skeletal muscle fibers, thereby exerting the greatest influence on the resting membrane potential?
options: Sodium (Na+)
Potassium (K+)
Calcium (Ca2+)
Intracellular organic anions (proteins)
questions.explain: At rest, background two-pore-domain (K2P) leak K+ channels are open, making K+ permeability roughly 50 to 100 times greater than Na+ permeability, so RMP sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential (EK).

open.q: Which diffusible ion possesses the greatest resting membrane permeability and exerts the strongest pull on the resting membrane potential?
accept: Potassium
K+
Potassium ion

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: Which equation calculates the equilibrium (Nernst) potential for a single permeant ion species across a cell membrane?
options: Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation
Poiseuille equation
Nernst equation
Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
questions.explain: The Nernst equation (E_ion = -(RT/zF) ln([ion]_in / [ion]_out), or ~61.5/z * log10([ion]_out/[ion]_in) at 37 C) gives the exact electrical potential that balances the chemical concentration gradient of a single ion.

open.q: Name the equation used to calculate the electrochemical equilibrium potential for a single ion across a membrane.
accept: Nernst equation

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: At 37 degrees Celsius, if the intracellular K+ concentration is 140 mM and extracellular K+ concentration is 3.5 mM, what is the approximate Nernst equilibrium potential for K+ (EK)?
options: +61.5 mV(positive 61.5 mV)
-61.5 mV(negative 61.5 mV)
0 mV
-98.5 mV(negative 98.5 mV)
questions.explain: EK = 61.5 * log10(3.5 / 140) = 61.5 * log10(0.025) = 61.5 * (-1.602) = -98.5 mV (typically ~ -90 to -95 mV at standard 4 mM extracellular K+).

open.q: Calculate the approximate Nernst equilibrium potential for K+ at 37 C when [K+]_out = 3.5 mM and [K+]_in = 140 mM.
accept: -98 mV
-99 mV

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: How does the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz (GHK) constant-field equation differ from the Nernst equation?
options: It calculates membrane potential when multiple monovalent ions (Na+, K+, Cl-) are simultaneously permeable, weighting each ion by its relative membrane permeability
It applies only to divalent cations such as Ca2+ and Mg2+
It ignores ion concentration gradients completely
It measures action potential conduction velocity in unmyelinated fibers
questions.explain: Because real membranes at rest are slightly permeable to Na+ and Cl- in addition to K+, the GHK equation sums each ion's concentration weighted by its relative permeability (PK, PNa, PCl) to determine actual resting Vm.

open.q: What additional factor does the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz (GHK) equation incorporate compared to the Nernst equation when determining resting membrane potential?
accept: Relative membrane permeabilities of multiple permeant ions (K+, Na+, Cl-)
Ion permeabilities across multiple ion species simultaneously

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: What is the direct electrogenic contribution of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump to the resting membrane potential, and what is its essential indirect role?
options: Direct contribution of -40 mV; indirect role is synthesizing ATP
Direct electrogenic contribution of about -3 to -4 mV (pumping 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in); indirect role is maintaining the steep transmembrane Na+ and K+ concentration gradients
Direct contribution of +20 mV; indirect role is opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Zero direct or indirect contribution to membrane potential
questions.explain: Extruding 3 positive charges (Na+) while importing 2 positive charges (K+) generates a small net outward current (~-4 mV), while its primary role is sustaining the chemical gradients on which K+ and Na+ diffusion potentials depend.

open.q: State the stoichiometry of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump and its approximate direct electrogenic voltage contribution to the resting membrane potential.
accept: 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in; approximately -3 to -4 mV
3 Na+ extruded, 2 K+ imported; about -4 mV

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: Why does resting membrane potential (~-70 to -85 mV) sit slightly less negative than the potassium equilibrium potential (EK ~ -94 mV)?
options: Because intracellular proteins carry a net positive charge
Because chloride is actively pumped out of all neurons
Because a small resting inward leak of Na+ (driven toward ENa ~ +60 mV) pulls the membrane potential slightly positive relative to EK
Because voltage-gated Ca2+ channels remain permanently open at rest
questions.explain: Even though PK is ~50-100 times larger than PNa at rest, the tiny resting Na+ conductance admits a steady inward Na+ leak that depolarizes Vm by ~10-15 mV above EK, balanced at steady state by the Na+/K+ pump.

open.q: Why is the resting membrane potential of a neuron (~-70 mV) less negative than the equilibrium potential for potassium (~-90 mV)?
accept: Small resting inward sodium leak permeability pulls Vm slightly toward ENa
Resting membrane has a small finite permeability to Na+ ions

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: How does acute hyperkalemia (elevated extracellular K+ concentration) affect the resting membrane potential of excitable cells?
options: It hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential to -120 mV
It has no effect on resting membrane potential
It shifts EK to +60 mV immediately
It reduces the outward K+ concentration gradient, making EK and the resting membrane potential less negative (depolarized)
questions.explain: Raising [K+]_out decreases the ratio [K+]_in / [K+]_out, shifting EK closer to 0 mV (depolarizing RMP), which initially brings Vm closer to threshold but with sustained depolarization inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels (causing weakness/paralysis).

open.q: How does an increase in extracellular potassium concentration (hyperkalemia) alter the resting membrane potential?
accept: Makes resting membrane potential less negative (depolarizes the membrane)
Depolarizes RMP because EK becomes less negative

questions.q: Which property distinguishes local graded (electrotonic) potentials from propagated action potentials?
options: Graded potentials vary in amplitude with stimulus strength, decay decrementally with distance, can summate, and have no refractory period
Graded potentials obey the all-or-none law
Graded potentials propagate without decrement over meters of axon
Graded potentials are always depolarizing and never hyperpolarizing
questions.explain: Receptor potentials, EPSPs, IPSPs, and end-plate potentials are graded responses mediated by ligand- or mechanically gated channels; they decay passively over short distances and summate spatially and temporally.

open.q: List three biophysical properties that distinguish graded potentials from action potentials.
accept: Amplitude proportional to stimulus strength, decremental spread, and ability to summate (no refractory period)
Graded amplitude, passive decay with distance, and summation

questions.q: What is the 'all-or-none' principle of the action potential?
options: Either every neuron in the brain fires simultaneously or none fires
Once membrane depolarization reaches or exceeds threshold potential, a full-amplitude, stereotyped action potential is generated; subthreshold stimuli produce no action potential
Action potential amplitude doubles whenever stimulus intensity doubles
All ion channels open simultaneously during every graded potential
questions.explain: Above threshold (typically ~-55 mV), the regenerative positive-feedback opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels drives peak amplitude to a fixed height regardless of how far above threshold the stimulus was.

open.q: Define the all-or-none law as it applies to neuronal action potentials.
accept: Any stimulus reaching or exceeding threshold generates a full-sized action potential of constant amplitude, whereas subthreshold stimuli elicit none
Threshold stimuli produce a maximal stereotyped action potential regardless of further increases in stimulus strength

questions.q: If all action potentials in a given sensory neuron have identical amplitude, how does the nervous system encode the intensity of a stronger stimulus?
options: By doubling the height of each individual spike
By reversing the polarity of the action potential
By increasing the frequency (firing rate) of action potentials and recruiting additional parallel nerve fibers (population coding)
By slowing conduction velocity down the axon
questions.explain: Stronger stimuli produce larger receptor/generator potentials that cross threshold more frequently during the relative refractory period (frequency coding) and activate higher-threshold neighboring axons (recruitment).

open.q: How does a nerve fiber encode stimulus intensity given that individual action potentials obey the all-or-none law?
accept: Frequency coding (higher action potential firing rate) and recruitment of additional nerve fibers
Increasing firing frequency and recruiting more axons

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: What is the firing threshold (threshold potential) in a typical mammalian neuron?
options: +35 mV
-90 mV
0 mV
Approximately -55 mV (about 15 mV depolarized from a -70 mV resting potential)
questions.explain: Threshold is the critical membrane voltage (~-55 mV) at which inward Na+ current through newly opened voltage-gated Na+ channels exceeds outward K+ leak current, triggering regenerative depolarization (Hodgkin cycle).

open.q: Define threshold potential in biophysical terms of inward and outward ionic currents.
accept: Membrane potential (~-55 mV) at which net inward Na+ current exceeds outward K+ current, initiating a self-regenerating action potential
Critical voltage where inward Na+ influx surpasses outward K+ efflux

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: Which gated channel conformational state explains the rapid depolarization upstroke (rising phase) of a neuronal action potential?
options: Voltage-gated Na+ channels rapidly open their activation (m) gates while their inactivation (h) gates are still open
Voltage-gated K+ channels open rapidly to admit K+ into the cell
Voltage-gated Na+ channels close both m and h gates simultaneously
Cl- channels open to extrude chloride ions
questions.explain: Depolarization to threshold rapidly swings open the voltage-sensitive activation (m) gates of Na+ channels within fractions of a millisecond, increasing PNa ~500- to 5,000-fold and driving Vm toward ENa (+60 mV).

open.q: Describe the status of the activation (m) and inactivation (h) gates of voltage-gated Na+ channels during the rising phase of the action potential.
accept: Both activation (m) gates and inactivation (h) gates are open
m gates open rapidly while h gates remain open

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: Which two channel events terminate the action potential peak (overshoot) and drive rapid repolarization back toward resting potential?
options: Opening of HCN funny channels and closure of K+ leak channels
Time-dependent closure of voltage-gated Na+ inactivation (h) gates and delayed opening of voltage-gated K+ channels
Activation of Na+/K+-ATPase alone
Opening of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
questions.explain: Shortly after opening, the intracellular ball-and-chain inactivation (h) gate plugs the Na+ channel pore, while slower delayed-rectifier voltage-gated K+ channels open to allow rapid K+ efflux.

open.q: State the two voltage-gated channel changes responsible for repolarization of the neuronal action potential.
accept: Inactivation (closure of h gates) of voltage-gated Na+ channels and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels
Na+ channel inactivation and delayed K+ channel activation

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: What causes the after-hyperpolarization (undershoot) observed immediately following repolarization in many neurons?
options: Persistent inward Na+ leak through open m gates
Influx of Ca2+ through L-type channels
Slow closure of voltage-gated K+ channels, which temporarily keeps PK elevated above resting levels so Vm approaches EK (~-90 mV)
Sudden cessation of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump
questions.explain: Because voltage-gated K+ channels close slowly after membrane repolarization, outward K+ conductance remains transiently higher than at rest, hyperpolarizing Vm closer to EK until K+ gates finish closing.

open.q: Why does the membrane potential briefly hyperpolarize past resting level during the after-hyperpolarization (undershoot) phase?
accept: Delayed closure of voltage-gated K+ channels keeps K+ permeability transiently higher than at rest, pulling Vm toward EK
Slow closing of voltage-gated potassium channels

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: In voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav), what is the functional difference between the 'closed (resting)' state at -70 mV and the 'inactivated' state at +30 mV?
options: Both states are identical and open immediately upon depolarization
In the closed state, both m and h gates are closed; in the inactivated state, both are open
In the closed state, the channel conducts K+; in the inactivated state, it conducts Ca2+

In the closed (resting) state, the m gate is closed and the h gate is open (capable of opening if depolarized); in the inactivated state, the m gate is open but the h gate plugs the pore (incapable of opening until repolarization resets h)
questions.explain: This three-state cycle (closed -> open -> inactivated -> closed) is the molecular basis of both unidirectional action potential propagation and the absolute refractory period.

open.q: Contrast the positions of the m (activation) and h (inactivation) gates of a voltage-gated Na+ channel in the resting closed state versus the inactivated state.
accept: Closed: m gate closed, h gate open; Inactivated: m gate open, h gate closed
Resting closed has closed m and open h; inactivated has open m and closed h

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: Which naturally occurring marine neurotoxin selectively blocks the outer pore of fast voltage-gated Na+ channels, abolishing action potential generation in nerves and skeletal muscle?
options: Tetrodotoxin (TTX, from pufferfish) and saxitoxin (from dinoflagellates)
Tetraethylammonium (TEA)
Alpha-bungarotoxin
Botulinum toxin
questions.explain: Tetrodotoxin (TTX) and saxitoxin bind the extracellular pore mouth of Nav channels, blocking Na+ influx during Phase 0; in contrast, tetraethylammonium (TEA) and 4-aminopyridine block voltage-gated K+ channels.

open.q: Name a marine toxin that specifically blocks fast voltage-gated sodium channels, and name an agent that blocks voltage-gated potassium channels.
accept: Tetrodotoxin (or saxitoxin) blocks Na+ channels; tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks K+ channels
TTX for Na+ channels and TEA for K+ channels

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: How do local anesthetic drugs (such as lidocaine and bupivacaine) block pain conduction along peripheral nociceptive axons?
options: They hyperpolarize the membrane by activating Na+/K+-ATPase

In their uncharged base form they cross the axonal membrane, become protonated intracellularly, and bind the inner pore of voltage-gated Na+ channels in the open/inactivated state (use-dependent blockade)
They destroy myelin sheaths permanently
They block postsynaptic GABA-A chloride channels
questions.explain: Weak-base local anesthetics cross the lipid bilayer un-ionized, then bind the intracellular S6 segment of Nav channels preferentially when channels are open or inactivated, preventing Na+ influx and slowing recovery from inactivation.

open.q: Explain the mechanism of action of local anesthetics like lidocaine on axonal ion channels and why their blockade is 'use-dependent'.
accept: They enter the axon and bind intracellularly to open/inactivated voltage-gated Na+ channels, blocking Na+ influx; rapidly firing axons have more open/inactivated channels
Intracellular blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels preferentially in open/inactivated states

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: Why are local anesthetics markedly less effective when injected into acutely infected, acidic inflamed tissue (such as a dental abscess)?
options: Bacteria metabolize lidocaine within 1 second
Acidic pH increases the ionized (protonated) fraction of the weak-base anesthetic outside the axon, preventing it from diffusing across the lipophilic axonal membrane
Inflammation increases axonal myelination tenfold
Low extracellular pH opens all voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
questions.explain: Because local anesthetics are weak bases (pKa ~7.6-8.9), low tissue pH shifts equilibrium toward the charged cationic form (BH+), which cannot penetrate the lipid membrane to reach its intracellular binding site on Nav channels.

open.q: Why does tissue acidosis (such as in an abscess) reduce the clinical efficacy of weak-base local anesthetics?
accept: Low pH increases the protonated (ionized) fraction of the drug, impairing its diffusion across the axonal cell membrane
Acidic environment traps the anesthetic in its charged form outside the neuron

questions.q: During which period of an action potential is it completely impossible to elicit a second action potential regardless of how strong the stimulus is?
options: Relative refractory period
After-hyperpolarization period
Absolute refractory period
Latent period
questions.explain: From threshold crossing through the peak and most of repolarization, nearly all voltage-gated Na+ channels are already open or inactivated (h gates closed), making a second spike impossible.

open.q: What is the absolute refractory period, and what channel state underlies it?
accept: Period during which no stimulus of any strength can trigger a second action potential, caused by inactivation (closed h gates) of voltage-gated Na+ channels
Time window where a new spike is impossible due to Na+ channel inactivation

questions.q: Why can a suprathreshold stimulus elicit a second action potential during the relative refractory period, and why does that second spike have a lower peak amplitude?
options: All Na+ channels have recovered and K+ channels are closed
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels replace Na+ channels completely
The Na+/K+ pump reverses direction

Some voltage-gated Na+ channels have recovered from inactivation (h gates reopened), while elevated K+ conductance (after-hyperpolarization) opposes depolarization so a stronger stimulus is needed and fewer Na+ channels are available
questions.explain: During late repolarization and undershoot, a fraction of Nav channels has reset to the resting state, but remaining open K+ channels hyperpolarize the cell and incomplete Nav recovery lowers the upstroke amplitude.

open.q: Explain the two ionic factors that require a stronger-than-normal stimulus to trigger an action potential during the relative refractory period.
accept: Partial recovery of voltage-gated Na+ channels from inactivation and persistent outward K+ current during after-hyperpolarization
Only a fraction of Na+ channels have reset and membrane is hyperpolarized by open K+ channels

questions.q: What is the physiological significance of the absolute refractory period in a single axon?
options: It limits the maximum firing frequency of the axon and ensures unidirectional forward propagation without backward re-excitation
It speeds up saltatory conduction across nodes of Ranvier
It prevents neurotransmitter exocytosis at the axon terminal
It converts electrical synapses into chemical synapses
questions.explain: If the absolute refractory period lasts 1 ms, maximum firing frequency cannot exceed 1,000 Hz (1 / 0.001 s); additionally, recently depolarized membrane behind the wave is refractory, forcing orthodromic conduction.

open.q: State two physiological functions of the absolute refractory period in nerve fibers.
accept: Sets the upper limit on action potential firing frequency and prevents retrograde (backward) propagation along the axon
Limits maximum firing rate and enforces unidirectional propagation

questions.q: What is 'accommodation' when an excitable membrane is exposed to a slowly rising subthreshold-to-threshold depolarizing current?
options: Rapid explosive firing of high-frequency action potentials

Failure to fire an action potential because slow depolarization gradually closes Na+ inactivation (h) gates and opens voltage-gated K+ channels before enough Na+ activation gates can open simultaneously
Focusing of the crystalline lens for near vision
Permanent destruction of the axon hillock
questions.explain: For a regenerative spike, depolarization must be fast enough to open m gates before slower h gates close and K+ channels activate; a very slow ramp current inactivates Nav channels silently without triggering a spike.

open.q: Explain the ionic mechanism of nerve accommodation in response to a slowly rising depolarizing stimulus.
accept: Slow depolarization inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels (closes h gates) and activates K+ channels gradually before threshold firing can occur
Gradual Na+ channel inactivation and K+ channel opening prevent action potential initiation

questions.q: Why does acute hypocalcemia (low extracellular ionized Ca2+) increase neuronal and skeletal muscle membrane excitability, leading to paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, and tetany?
options: Ca2+ directly enters through fast Na+ channels to depolarize the cell
Hypocalcemia activates the Na+/K+-ATPase pump tenfold

Extracellular Ca2+ normally screens negative surface charges on the outer membrane; low Ca2+ shifts the voltage-gating threshold of Na+ channels closer to resting potential so they open with minimal depolarization
Hypocalcemia blocks all voltage-gated K+ channels permanently
questions.explain: Divalent Ca2+ ions bind negative phospholipid/protein charges on the external membrane surface, stabilizing voltage-gated Na+ channels; reducing [Ca2+]_out makes the voltage sensor perceive a depolarized field, lowering firing threshold and causing spontaneous discharges.

open.q: Explain how hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability and causes tetany.
accept: Reduced extracellular Ca2+ decreases external membrane charge screening, shifting voltage-gated Na+ channel activation threshold closer to resting membrane potential
Low extracellular Ca2+ lowers the activation threshold of voltage-gated Na+ channels, making nerves hyperexcitable

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: Where in a typical multipolar neuron are action potentials normally initiated, and why?
options: At the tip of distal dendrites, because they have the highest myelin thickness
At the soma nucleus, because nuclear pores admit Na+
At the postsynaptic membrane, because glutamate opens Nav channels
At the axon hillock (initial segment), because it has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels and therefore the lowest firing threshold
questions.explain: Summated EPSPs and IPSPs spread electrotonically to the axon initial segment (axon hillock), where dense clustering of Nav1.6 channels lowers threshold to ~-55 mV (versus ~-35 mV in soma/dendrites).

open.q: Which anatomical region of a multipolar neuron has the lowest threshold for action potential initiation, and what structural feature accounts for this?
accept: Axon hillock (initial segment), due to its high density of voltage-gated Na+ channels
Initial segment of the axon; dense voltage-gated Na+ channels

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: What is the length constant (space constant, lambda) of an axon, and how is it defined mathematically in terms of membrane resistance (rm) and internal axial resistance (ri)?
options: Distance over which a passive electrotonic potential decays to 37% (1/e) of its original amplitude; lambda = square root of (rm / ri)
Time required for membrane potential to reach 63% of its final value; lambda = rm x cm
Total physical length of the spinal cord; lambda = ri / rm
Diameter of a node of Ranvier; lambda = 1 / rm
questions.explain: lambda = sqrt(rm / ri). A larger length constant means current spreads farther along the axon before leaking out across the membrane, improving conduction efficiency.

open.q: Define the membrane length constant (lambda) and write its formula in terms of membrane resistance (rm) and internal axial resistance (ri).
accept: Distance at which a passive potential falls to 37% (1/e) of its initial value; lambda = sqrt(rm / ri)
lambda = square root of (rm / ri); distance for 63% decay

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: What is the membrane time constant (tau), and how does a shorter time constant affect action potential propagation?
options: tau = rm / ri; a shorter time constant slows conduction velocity
tau = rm x cm (membrane resistance times membrane capacitance); a shorter tau allows the membrane to charge and reach threshold faster, increasing conduction velocity
tau = cm / rm; a shorter tau prevents saltatory conduction
tau = ENa - EK; a shorter tau abolishes the refractory period
questions.explain: tau = rm * cm is the time for Vm to reach 63% (1 - 1/e) of its steady-state change during a constant current step; myelination dramatically reduces membrane capacitance (cm), shortening tau so nodes depolarize rapidly.

open.q: Write the formula for the membrane time constant (tau) and explain how myelination alters membrane capacitance (cm) to speed conduction.
accept: tau = rm x cm; myelin thickens the insulator and decreases membrane capacitance (cm), allowing faster depolarization
tau = rm * cm; myelination reduces capacitance

questions.q: Which glial cells synthesize the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) versus the central nervous system (CNS)?
options: Astrocytes in PNS; microglia in CNS
Ependymal cells in PNS; satellite cells in CNS
Schwann cells in PNS (one cell per internode); oligodendrocytes in CNS (one cell myelinating up to 30-50 internodes)
Oligodendrocytes in PNS; Schwann cells in CNS
questions.explain: Schwann cells wrap single peripheral axon segments, whereas oligodendrocytes extend multiple processes to myelinate segments of several CNS axons simultaneously.

open.q: Name the myelin-forming glial cells in the peripheral nervous system and in the central nervous system.
accept: Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS
PNS: Schwann cells; CNS: oligodendrocytes

questions.q: What is saltatory conduction, and what are its two major physiological advantages over continuous conduction in unmyelinated fibers?
options: Backward conduction of impulses; doubles ATP consumption and shrinks axon diameter
Chemical diffusion of neurotransmitters inside the axon; eliminates the need for Na+ channels
Continuous opening of Na+ channels along the entire internode; prevents all-or-none firing

Jumping of action potentials from one node of Ranvier to the next; increases conduction velocity up to 50- to 100-fold and conserves metabolic ATP energy by restricting transmembrane ion fluxes to nodes
questions.explain: Myelin increases transverse membrane resistance (rm) and lowers capacitance (cm), allowing local currents to jump rapidly between Nav-rich nodes of Ranvier while dramatically reducing the Na+/K+-ATPase workload.

open.q: State the two primary physiological advantages of saltatory conduction in myelinated nerve fibers.
accept: Much faster conduction velocity and conservation of metabolic energy (ATP) because ion exchange occurs only at nodes of Ranvier
Increased conduction speed and reduced ATP expenditure by Na+/K+-ATPase

questions.q: Why does demyelination (as in multiple sclerosis or Guillain-Barre syndrome) slow or block action potential conduction along affected axons?
options: Loss of myelin decreases transverse membrane resistance (rm) and increases membrane capacitance (cm), causing current leakage across internodes and failure to depolarize the next node to threshold (conduction block)
Demyelination removes all voltage-gated K+ channels from the soma
Demyelination reverses the Nernst potential of Na+ to -90 mV
Demyelination causes excessive myelin thickening at nodes of Ranvier
questions.explain: Without myelin insulation, the length constant (lambda) shrinks and time constant (tau) lengthens; internodal membrane also has sparse Nav channels, so local current dissipates before reaching the next node.

open.q: Explain in terms of cable properties (rm, cm, and length constant) why demyelination causes conduction slowing or conduction block.
accept: Loss of myelin lowers membrane resistance (rm) and raises capacitance (cm), shortening the length constant so current leaks out before reaching the next node of Ranvier
Decreased rm and increased cm reduce lambda, causing current dissipation and failure to excite the next node

questions.q: According to the Erlanger-Gasser classification of mammalian nerve fibers, which fiber group has the largest diameter (13-20 micrometers), thickest myelin, and fastest conduction velocity (80-120 m/s)?
options: Type C unmyelinated fibers
Type A-alpha fibers
Type B preganglionic autonomic fibers
Type A-delta fibers
questions.explain: A-alpha (Group Ia and Ib) fibers innervate skeletal muscle extrafusal fibers, primary muscle spindle endings, and Golgi tendon organs, conducting at 80-120 m/s.

open.q: Which Erlanger-Gasser nerve fiber type exhibits the largest diameter and fastest conduction velocity (80-120 m/s), and name one structure it innervates?
accept: A-alpha fibers; skeletal extrafusal muscle fibers, muscle spindles (Ia), or Golgi tendon organs (Ib)
Type A-alpha; alpha motor neurons or primary proprioceptors

questions.q: Which nerve fiber types transmit fast, sharp, well-localized 'first pain' versus slow, dull, aching, poorly localized 'second pain'?
options: A-alpha fibers transmit fast pain; B fibers transmit slow pain
A-beta fibers transmit fast pain; A-alpha fibers transmit slow pain
Thinly myelinated A-delta fibers (5-30 m/s) transmit fast sharp pain; unmyelinated C fibers (0.5-2 m/s) transmit slow burning/aching pain
Type C fibers transmit fast pain; A-delta fibers transmit slow pain
questions.explain: A-delta nociceptors carry rapid pricking/sharp pain and cold sensations, while unmyelinated C polymodal nociceptors (and postganglionic sympathetic fibers) carry slow, diffuse pain and warmth.

open.q: Contrast the nerve fiber types, myelination status, and conduction velocities mediating fast sharp pain versus slow dull pain.
accept: Fast pain: thinly myelinated A-delta fibers (5-30 m/s); Slow pain: unmyelinated C fibers (0.5-2 m/s)
A-delta (myelinated, faster) vs C fibers (unmyelinated, slowest)

questions.q: Which nerve fiber types are most susceptible to conduction block by hypoxia, mechanical pressure, and local anesthetics, respectively?
options: C fibers are most sensitive to pressure; A-alpha fibers are most sensitive to local anesthetics
All nerve fibers show identical susceptibility to hypoxia, pressure, and local anesthetics
B fibers are most sensitive to pressure; C fibers are most sensitive to hypoxia

Type B fibers are most susceptible to hypoxia; Type A (large myelinated) fibers are most susceptible to mechanical pressure; Type C (small unmyelinated) fibers are most susceptible to local anesthetics
questions.explain: Classic differential vulnerability: Hypoxia affects B > A > C; Pressure affects A > B > C (why crossing legs causes numbness/foot drop before pain loss); Local anesthetics block C > B > A (loss of pain/temperature before touch/motor).

open.q: Identify which nerve fiber type (A, B, or C) is most sensitive to: (1) hypoxia, (2) mechanical pressure, and (3) local anesthetics.
accept: Hypoxia: B fibers; Pressure: A fibers; Local anesthetics: C fibers

questions.q: What is the functional structural unit of a skeletal myofibril extending from one Z-disc (Z-line) to the next Z-disc?
options: Sarcomere
Sarcoplasmic reticulum
Motor end-plate
Perimysium
questions.explain: The sarcomere (~2.0-2.2 um at rest) contains overlapping thick (myosin) and thin (actin, tropomyosin, troponin) filaments bounded at both ends by Z-discs.

open.q: Name the basic contractile unit of striated muscle bounded by two adjacent Z-discs.
accept: Sarcomere

questions.q: During isotonic shortening of a skeletal muscle sarcomere, what happens to the widths of the A band, I band, and H zone?
options: The A band shortens by 50% while the I band and H zone widen
The A band remains constant in width (equal to thick filament length), while both the I band and H zone narrow as thin filaments slide inward
All three bands (A, I, and H) widen proportionally
The Z-discs move farther apart
questions.explain: In the sliding-filament mechanism, neither thick nor thin filaments change physical length; the A band (length of myosin thick filaments) stays constant, whereas the I band (actin-only zone) and H zone (myosin-only central zone) shorten.

open.q: State what happens to the widths of the A band, I band, and H zone when a skeletal muscle sarcomere contracts.
accept: A band stays the same width; I band and H zone shorten (narrow)
A band unchanged, I band and H zone narrow

questions.q: Which structural protein anchors thick myosin filaments to the Z-disc and acts as a molecular spring responsible for passive elasticity of resting skeletal muscle?
options: Dystrophin
Troponin I
Titin (connectin)
Nebulin
questions.explain: Titin is the largest known human protein (~3-4 MDa), spanning half a sarcomere from Z-disc to M-line to center thick filaments and provide passive resting tension; nebulin acts as a molecular ruler along thin actin filaments.

open.q: Name the giant elastic sarcomeric protein that connects myosin thick filaments to the Z-disc and generates passive muscle elasticity.
accept: Titin
Connectin

questions.q: In skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, how does depolarization of the transverse (T) tubule trigger Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)?
options: Extracellular Ca2+ enters through T-tubule channels and diffuses to troponin C
Acetylcholine enters the T-tubule and binds directly to calsequestrin
T-tubule depolarization activates adenylate cyclase to phosphorylate myosin

Voltage-sensing dihydropyridine (DHP) receptors in the T-tubule membrane undergo a conformational change that mechanically pulls open linked ryanodine receptor (RyR1) Ca2+ release channels on the SR terminal cisternae
questions.explain: In skeletal muscle (triads at the A-I junction), DHP receptors (Cav1.1) are physically coupled to RyR1 channels on SR terminal cisternae, triggering rapid Ca2+ release without requiring extracellular Ca2+ influx.

open.q: Describe the physical coupling between dihydropyridine (DHP) receptors and ryanodine receptors (RyR1) during skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling.
accept: T-tubule depolarization causes a conformational change in voltage-sensing DHP receptors that mechanically opens linked RyR1 Ca2+ release channels on the SR
Direct mechanical linkage between T-tubule DHP sensors and SR RyR1 channels releases Ca2+

questions.q: Which subunit of the troponin complex binds Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to move tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin?
options: Troponin C (TnC)
Troponin I (TnI)
Troponin T (TnT)
Calsequestrin
questions.explain: Troponin T binds tropomyosin, Troponin I inhibits actomyosin interaction at rest, and Troponin C binds up to four Ca2+ ions to shift tropomyosin and uncover actin active sites.

open.q: State the specific functions of the three troponin subunits: TnT, TnI, and TnC.
accept: TnT binds tropomyosin, TnI inhibits actin-myosin binding, and TnC binds calcium ions
TnT: tropomyosin binding; TnI: inhibitory; TnC: calcium binding

questions.q: In the skeletal muscle cross-bridge cycle, what specific molecular event requires the binding of a fresh ATP molecule to the myosin head?
options: Generation of the power stroke
Detachment of the myosin head from the actin filament (breaking the rigor state)
Release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Depolarization of the motor end-plate
questions.explain: ATP binding reduces myosin's affinity for actin so the cross-bridge detaches; ATP hydrolysis to ADP + Pi then cocks the myosin head into its high-energy conformation, and Pi release triggers the power stroke.

open.q: What is the direct role of ATP binding to the myosin head during the cross-bridge cycle, and why does rigor mortis occur after death?
accept: ATP binding detaches myosin from actin; after death, ATP depletion leaves myosin heads locked onto actin in rigor
Detachment of myosin cross-bridges from actin; lack of ATP prevents detachment

questions.q: How does skeletal muscle relaxation occur once motor neuron action potentials cease?
options: Ca2+ diffuses passively out of the muscle fiber into blood plasma
Myosin heads degrade all intracellular troponin C
SERCA (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase) actively pumps Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (where calsequestrin binds it), lowering cytosolic Ca2+ so tropomyosin re-covers actin
Voltage-gated Na+ channels pump Ca2+ into the T-tubules
questions.explain: Active re-sequestration of Ca2+ into the SR by SERCA (requiring 1 ATP per 2 Ca2+ pumped) drops cytosolic [Ca2+] back below 10^-7 M, allowing Ca2+ to dissociate from TnC and tropomyosin to block myosin binding.

open.q: Name the ATP-dependent pump responsible for sequestering Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to initiate skeletal muscle relaxation, and the Ca2+-binding storage protein inside the SR lumen.
accept: SERCA (SR Ca2+-ATPase) and calsequestrin
Sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase and calsequestrin

questions.q: Why does skeletal muscle generate maximal active isometric tension at an optimal resting sarcomere length of approximately 2.0 to 2.2 micrometers?
options: At 2.0-2.2 um, thick and thin filaments do not overlap at all
At 2.0-2.2 um, titin completely prevents cross-bridge formation
At 2.0-2.2 um, the Z-discs collide with the thick filaments
At 2.0-2.2 um, there is optimal overlap between myosin cross-bridges and actin filaments without thin-filament double overlap or thick-filament collision with Z-discs
questions.explain: Overstretching beyond ~3.6 um eliminates overlap (zero active tension), whereas shortening below ~2.0 um causes opposing thin filaments to overlap and thick filaments to abut Z-discs, reducing force (length-tension relationship).

open.q: Explain the sarcomere length-tension relationship in skeletal muscle.
accept: Active tension is maximal at optimal sarcomere length (~2.0-2.2 um) where cross-bridge overlap is greatest, and falls when overstretched (less overlap) or overly shortened (filament interference)
Force depends on degree of thick-thin filament overlap, peaking at ~2.0-2.2 um

questions.q: According to Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity relationship for concentric skeletal muscle contraction, when is shortening velocity maximal (Vmax)?
options: When the external load (afterload) is zero
When the external load equals maximal isometric tension (Po)
During an eccentric lengthening contraction
When ATP concentration drops to zero
questions.explain: Shortening velocity varies inversely with external load: Vmax occurs at zero load (governed by myosin heavy-chain ATPase rate), whereas velocity equals zero when load equals maximal isometric force (Po).

open.q: Describe the relationship between external load and shortening velocity in a concentrically contracting skeletal muscle.
accept: Shortening velocity decreases hyperbolically as external load increases, reaching Vmax at zero load and zero velocity at maximal isometric load
Inverse hyperbolic relationship: highest velocity at zero load, zero velocity at isometric load

questions.sub: Motor Units, Summation, and Muscle Fiber Types
questions.q: What is a motor unit, and how does motor unit size relate to precision of movement?
options: A single muscle fiber innervated by ten motor neurons; large units produce fine movements

A single alpha motor neuron together with all the skeletal muscle fibers it innervates; small motor units (e.g., 3-10 fibers in extraocular muscles) allow fine graded control, whereas large units (e.g., 1,000+ fibers in gastrocnemius) generate gross power
A group of sensory spindles in a tendon; controls blood flow
A bundle of smooth muscle cells joined by gap junctions
questions.explain: All muscle fibers within a single motor unit share the same histochemical fiber type and contract synchronously whenever their alpha motor neuron fires.

open.q: Define a motor unit and compare the innervation ratio in extraocular muscles versus postural limb muscles.
accept: One alpha motor neuron and all skeletal muscle fibers it innervates; extraocular muscles have small units (~3-10 fibers) for fine control, while limb muscles have large units (hundreds to >1,000 fibers)
Single alpha motor neuron plus the muscle fibers it supplies; low ratio in eye/hand muscles vs high ratio in postural muscles

questions.sub: Motor Units, Summation, and Muscle Fiber Types
questions.q: What does Henneman's size principle state about the recruitment of motor units during progressively increasing voluntary muscle effort?
options: Large, fast-fatigable Type IIb motor units are always recruited first
Motor units are recruited randomly regardless of axon diameter

Small, low-threshold alpha motor neurons innervating slow oxidative (Type I) fatigue-resistant fibers are recruited first, followed progressively by larger motor neurons innervating Type IIa and Type IIx/IIb fast fibers
All motor units fire simultaneously even during light finger tapping
questions.explain: Because small motor neurons have smaller surface area and higher input resistance (Ohm's law: V = I * R), a given synaptic input depolarizes them to threshold first, ensuring smooth force gradation and fatigue resistance for posture.

open.q: State Henneman's size principle of motor unit recruitment and explain its biophysical basis.
accept: Smaller motor neurons (Type I slow oxidative units) are recruited before larger ones (Type II fast units) because smaller neurons have higher input resistance and depolarize more easily
Recruitment proceeds from smallest to largest alpha motor neurons due to higher input resistance of small somata

questions.sub: Motor Units, Summation, and Muscle Fiber Types
questions.q: How does temporal (wave) summation produce complete tetanus in a skeletal muscle fiber?
options: Because skeletal muscle has a 250 ms plateau phase
Because motor neurons stop releasing acetylcholine during tetanus
Because extracellular sodium enters through T-tubules to bind troponin

Because the skeletal muscle action potential (~2-5 ms) is much shorter than the mechanical twitch (~20-100 ms), allowing rapid repetitive stimuli to trigger new Ca2+ release before SERCA can reuptake Ca2+, maintaining saturating cytosolic Ca2+
questions.explain: Unlike cardiac muscle (where the 200 ms refractory period prevents summation), skeletal muscle's brief refractory period permits high-frequency stimulation to fuse twitches into smooth maximal tetanic tension (~3-4 times single twitch force).

open.q: Why can skeletal muscle undergo tetanic summation whereas cardiac muscle cannot?
accept: Skeletal muscle action potential and refractory period (~2-5 ms) are much shorter than its mechanical contraction, allowing repetitive Ca2+ release to summate
Brief refractory period in skeletal muscle vs prolonged plateau refractory period in cardiac muscle

questions.sub: Motor Units, Summation, and Muscle Fiber Types
questions.q: Which characteristics distinguish Type I (slow oxidative, red) skeletal muscle fibers from Type IIb/IIx (fast glycolytic, white) fibers?
options: Type I fibers have high myoglobin, abundant mitochondria, rich capillary density, slow myosin ATPase, and high fatigue resistance; Type IIb/IIx fibers have low myoglobin, abundant glycogen/glycolytic enzymes, fast myosin ATPase, and rapid fatigue
Type I fibers fatigue within 5 seconds and rely solely on anaerobic glycolysis
Type IIb fibers contain ten times more myoglobin and mitochondria than Type I fibers
Type I fibers lack sarcoplasmic reticulum completely
questions.explain: Type I postural/endurance fibers sustain aerobic ATP generation without fatigue, whereas Type IIb/IIx sprint/power fibers generate rapid peak force via fast myosin heavy-chain ATPase and anaerobic glycolysis.

open.q: Contrast Type I (slow oxidative) and Type IIx/IIb (fast glycolytic) skeletal muscle fibers across three structural or metabolic features.
accept: Type I: high myoglobin, many mitochondria, slow myosin ATPase, fatigue-resistant; Type IIb/IIx: low myoglobin, high glycogen/glycolysis, fast myosin ATPase, fatigues quickly
Red oxidative fatigue-resistant slow fibers vs white glycolytic rapidly fatiguing fast fibers

questions.q: Which intracellular Ca2+-binding regulatory protein replaces troponin in smooth muscle to initiate contraction?
options: Calsequestrin
Calmodulin
Dystrophin
Titin
questions.explain: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; instead, cytosolic Ca2+ binds calmodulin (4 Ca2+ per calmodulin), and the Ca2+-calmodulin complex activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) to phosphorylate the 20-kDa myosin regulatory light chain.

open.q: Trace the intracellular biochemical cascade from elevated cytosolic Ca2+ to myosin cross-bridge cycling in smooth muscle.
accept: Ca2+ binds calmodulin -> activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) -> phosphorylates myosin light chains -> enables actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling
Ca2+-calmodulin activates MLCK to phosphorylate myosin heads

questions.q: How do unitary (visceral) smooth muscle and multiunit smooth muscle differ in their electrical coupling and neural control?
options: Unitary smooth muscle lacks gap junctions and has individual nerve endings on every cell; multiunit smooth muscle contracts as a single syncytium
Both unitary and multiunit smooth muscles contain sarcomeres and T-tubules

Unitary smooth muscle (gut, uterus, ureter) has abundant gap junctions allowing spontaneous pacemaker waves to spread syncytially, whereas multiunit smooth muscle (iris, ciliary muscle, piloerectors, vas deferens) consists of discrete motor-like fibers with few gap junctions controlled finely by autonomic nerves
Multiunit smooth muscle is found only in the stomach wall
questions.explain: Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle exhibits myogenic pacemaker slow waves and stretch-induced contraction across gap-junction-coupled sheets, whereas multiunit smooth muscle requires discrete autonomic varicosity stimulation.

open.q: Compare unitary (visceral) and multiunit smooth muscle in terms of gap junctions, spontaneous activity, and anatomical examples.
accept: Unitary has numerous gap junctions and spontaneous syncytial contractions (GI tract, uterus); multiunit has few gap junctions and discrete neural control (iris, ciliary body, piloerector muscles)
Syncytial gap-junction-coupled visceral muscle vs independently innervated multiunit fibers

questions.q: What is the 'latch-bridge' mechanism in vascular and visceral smooth muscle?
options: Rapid hydrolysis of 100 ATP molecules per cross-bridge cycle
Irreversible death of smooth muscle cells during vasoconstriction
Opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels during sleep

Dephosphorylation of attached myosin cross-bridges by myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP) while still bound to actin, drastically slowing detachment rate so tonic force is maintained for hours with minimal ATP consumption
questions.explain: The latch state allows tonic sphincters and arterioles to sustain continuous tension at ~1/100th to 1/300th the ATP cost of skeletal muscle.

open.q: Explain the latch-bridge phenomenon in smooth muscle and its physiological advantage.
accept: Dephosphorylated myosin heads remain attached to actin with very slow cycling, sustaining prolonged tonic contraction with minimal ATP expenditure
Slowly detaching dephosphorylated cross-bridges maintain sustained tension at very low energy cost

questions.q: How does Rho-kinase (ROCK) activation (such as by angiotensin II or endothelin-1) produce 'calcium sensitization' in vascular smooth muscle?
options: Rho-kinase phosphorylates and inhibits myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP), keeping myosin light chains phosphorylated and contracted even without a further rise in cytosolic Ca2+
Rho-kinase pumps Ca2+ out of the cell via the plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase
Rho-kinase degrades calmodulin in the cytoplasm
Rho-kinase opens BKCa potassium channels to hyperpolarize the membrane
questions.explain: Agonists coupled to G12/13 activate RhoA -> Rho-kinase, which inhibits MLCP; conversely, nitric oxide/cGMP activates protein kinase G (PKG) to stimulate MLCP (calcium desensitization and vasodilation).

open.q: Explain how Rho-kinase induces calcium sensitization in vascular smooth muscle.
accept: Rho-kinase inhibits myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP), enhancing myosin light-chain phosphorylation and contraction at a constant Ca2+ level
Inhibition of MLCP by Rho-kinase increases force sensitivity to Ca2+

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: In mammalian neurons, what are the approximate intracellular versus extracellular concentrations of Na+, K+, and Cl-?
options: Na+: 145 mM out vs 12-15 mM in; K+: 4 mM out vs 140-150 mM in; Cl-: 105-110 mM out vs 5-10 mM in
Na+: 145 mM in vs 12 mM out; K+: 140 mM out vs 4 mM in; Cl-: 105 mM in vs 5 mM out
All three ions have equal concentrations of 100 mM inside and outside
K+ is 145 mM outside and Na+ is 140 mM inside
questions.explain: Na+ and Cl- are predominantly extracellular (~145 mM and ~108 mM), whereas K+ (~145 mM) and negatively charged organic proteins/phosphates are predominantly intracellular.

open.q: Give the approximate extracellular and intracellular concentrations (in mM) for Na+ and K+ in mammalian neurons.
accept: Na+: ~145 mM extracellular, ~12-15 mM intracellular; K+: ~4 mM extracellular, ~140-150 mM intracellular
ECF Na+ 145 mM / ICF Na+ 15 mM; ECF K+ 4 mM / ICF K+ 140 mM

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: What is the Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium, and why do living cells require an active Na+/K+-ATPase pump to avoid osmotic lysis from the Donnan effect?
options: Non-diffusible intracellular anionic proteins attract excess diffusible cations (Na+ and K+) into the cell, creating an osmotic gradient that would draw water in and swell/burst the cell unless the Na+/K+ pump continuously extrudes Na+
It describes the rapid diffusion of oxygen across alveolar membranes
It causes potassium to leave the cell until intracellular K+ equals zero
It equalizes calcium concentrations between the nucleus and mitochondria
questions.explain: Because trapped intracellular proteins carry negative charges, passive Gibbs-Donnan distribution accumulates higher total osmotically active ions inside than outside; the Na+/K+ pump acts as a 'double-Donnan' mechanism making the membrane effectively impermeable to Na+ to keep cell volume constant.

open.q: Explain why non-diffusible intracellular anions (Gibbs-Donnan effect) would cause cell swelling if the Na+/K+-ATPase pump were inhibited (e.g., by ouabain).
accept: Intracellular impermeant anions attract excess cations and water into the cell; blocking Na+/K+-ATPase allows Na+ and Cl- entry followed by osmotic water influx and cell swelling
Donnan distribution increases intracellular osmolarity, which is normally counteracted by active Na+ extrusion

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: What is the 'driving force' (electrochemical driving force, V_DF) acting on a permeant ion across a cell membrane?
options: Vm + E_ion
Vm - E_ion (the difference between the actual membrane potential and that ion's Nernst equilibrium potential)
E_Na / E_K
Membrane capacitance divided by resistance
questions.explain: Net ionic current I_ion = g_ion * (Vm - E_ion). At rest (Vm = -70 mV), K+ has a small outward driving force (-70 - (-90) = +20 mV), whereas Na+ has a huge inward driving force (-70 - (+60) = -130 mV).

open.q: Write the formula for the electrochemical driving force on an ion and calculate the driving force on Na+ at Vm = -70 mV if ENa = +60 mV.
accept: Vm - E_ion; -130 mV (inward driving force)
Vm minus ENa = -130 mV

questions.q: What is the precise definition of 'depolarization' versus 'hyperpolarization' of an excitable cell membrane?
options: Depolarization makes membrane potential more negative; hyperpolarization makes it less negative
Both terms mean returning membrane potential to -70 mV
Depolarization is a shift in membrane potential toward a less negative (more positive) value than resting potential; hyperpolarization is a shift toward a more negative value than resting potential
Depolarization occurs only when Cl- enters the cell
questions.explain: Because resting potential is polarized (-70 mV), moving toward 0 mV (e.g., -70 to -50 mV) reduces polarization (depolarization), whereas moving to -85 mV increases polarization (hyperpolarization).

open.q: Distinguish depolarization, repolarization, and hyperpolarization in terms of membrane potential changes relative to a -70 mV resting state.
accept: Depolarization: less negative than -70 mV; Repolarization: return toward -70 mV; Hyperpolarization: more negative than -70 mV
Depolarization moves toward 0 mV, repolarization restores resting negative potential, hyperpolarization becomes more negative than rest

questions.q: In strength-duration curves for electrical excitation of a nerve or muscle fiber, how are 'rheobase' and 'chronaxie' defined?
options: Rheobase is the shortest duration at zero voltage; chronaxie is maximal voltage
Rheobase is action potential peak height; chronaxie is total duration of the spike
Rheobase is conduction velocity; chronaxie is axon diameter

Rheobase is the minimum constant current strength required to excite a tissue regardless of stimulus duration; chronaxie is the minimum duration required to excite the tissue using a current of twice rheobase strength
questions.explain: Chronaxie (time required at 2x rheobase) is a standard index of tissue excitability: fast large myelinated axons have short chronaxies (~0.1-0.3 ms), whereas denervated skeletal muscle or smooth muscle has a much longer chronaxie.

open.q: Define rheobase and chronaxie on an excitable tissue's strength-duration curve.
accept: Rheobase: minimum current intensity that elicits excitation given an infinitely long duration; Chronaxie: minimum stimulus duration needed at twice rheobase intensity
Rheobase is threshold current at long duration; chronaxie is threshold duration at 2x rheobase

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: Why does the peak of a neuronal action potential (~+30 to +35 mV) fall short of the theoretical sodium Nernst equilibrium potential (ENa ~ +60 mV)?
options: Because Na+ inactivation (h) gates begin closing and delayed-rectifier K+ channels begin opening before Vm can reach +60 mV, creating opposing outward K+ current
Because intracellular Na+ concentration suddenly rises to 500 mM during a single spike
Because the Na+/K+ pump reverses during the peak
Because voltage-gated Cl- channels open at +30 mV
questions.explain: During a single action potential, only ~1 in 100,000 intracellular ions changes concentration, so ENa stays near +60 mV; however, rapid Nav inactivation and Kv activation shift the chord conductance back toward EK before Vm reaches ENa.

open.q: Explain why the neuronal action potential overshoot peaks around +35 mV rather than reaching ENa (+60 mV).
accept: Na+ channels rapidly inactivate (h gates close) and voltage-gated K+ channels open before Vm reaches ENa
Early Na+ channel inactivation and rising outward K+ conductance prevent Vm from reaching +60 mV

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: How many transmembrane alpha-helical segments (S1-S6) comprise each of the four homologous domains of a voltage-gated Na+ channel alpha-subunit, and which segment acts as the primary positively charged voltage sensor?
options: Two segments (S1-S2); S1 is the voltage sensor
Six segments (S1-S6) per domain; the S4 segment (containing positively charged arginine/lysine residues every third position) moves outward upon depolarization to open the channel
Ten segments (S1-S10); S10 is the voltage sensor
Four segments (S1-S4); S2 is the selectivity filter
questions.explain: The Nav alpha-subunit has four domains (I-IV), each with 6 transmembrane helices (S1-S6); S4 is the voltage sensor, the S5-S6 P-loop forms the DEKA Na+-selectivity filter, and the cytoplasmic linker between domains III and IV forms the hinged-lid inactivation (h) gate.

open.q: Identify the voltage-sensing transmembrane segment and the intracellular inactivation gate linker of a voltage-gated Na+ channel alpha-subunit.
accept: S4 transmembrane segment is the voltage sensor; the cytoplasmic linker between domains III and IV forms the inactivation gate
S4 helix (voltage sensor) and III-IV intracellular loop (inactivation gate)

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: What happens to the duration of a neuronal action potential if voltage-gated delayed-rectifier K+ channels are pharmacologically blocked with tetraethylammonium (TEA)?
options: No action potential can be initiated at all
The action potential becomes 10 times shorter

The Phase 0 upstroke still occurs normally, but repolarization is markedly delayed (prolonging action potential duration) because repolarization must rely solely on Na+ inactivation and passive K+ leak
The resting membrane potential jumps to +60 mV
questions.explain: Because voltage-gated K+ channels do not participate in Phase 0, TEA leaves the upstroke intact while slowing repolarization and abolishing the after-hyperpolarization undershoot.

open.q: Describe how blocking voltage-gated K+ channels with tetraethylammonium (TEA) alters the shape of a neuronal action potential.
accept: Upstroke (Phase 0) is unaffected, but repolarization is slowed/prolonged and after-hyperpolarization is abolished
Prolongs repolarization phase and eliminates the undershoot while leaving depolarization intact

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: How does increasing axon diameter (for example, in the squid giant axon up to 500-1,000 micrometers) increase action potential conduction velocity?
options: It increases internal axial resistance (ri)
It decreases the length constant (lambda)
It eliminates all voltage-gated Na+ channels

It markedly decreases internal longitudinal (axial) resistance (ri, which scales inversely with cross-sectional area r^2), increasing the length constant (lambda) so local depolarizing currents spread farther ahead
questions.explain: Because axial resistance ri scales as 1/r^2 while membrane resistance rm scales as 1/r, the length constant lambda = sqrt(rm/ri) increases proportionally to the square root of radius, speeding longitudinal current spread.

open.q: Explain why large-diameter axons conduct action potentials faster than small-diameter axons.
accept: Larger diameter lowers internal axial resistance (ri), increasing the length constant so local currents depolarize downstream membrane faster
Reduced longitudinal cytoplasmic resistance increases passive current spread ahead of the active zone

questions.q: Where are voltage-gated Na+ channels concentrated in a healthy myelinated axon, and where are voltage-gated K+ channels predominantly located?
options: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are densely clustered at the nodes of Ranvier (~1,000-2,000/um2), whereas voltage-gated K+ channels are largely sequestered under the myelin in the juxtaparanodal region
Both Na+ and K+ channels are uniformly absent from nodes of Ranvier
Na+ channels are restricted exclusively to the internodal myelin sheath
K+ channels outnumber Na+ channels 100:1 at the nodes of Ranvier
questions.explain: Ankyrin-G anchors dense Nav1.6 channels at nodes of Ranvier for rapid inward current generation, while juxtaparanodal Kv1 channels under the paranodal seal help stabilize internodal resting potential (and become exposed during demyelination, worsening conduction block).

open.q: Compare the distribution of voltage-gated Na+ channels and voltage-gated K+ channels along a myelinated axon.
accept: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are densely clustered at nodes of Ranvier, whereas voltage-gated K+ channels are concentrated beneath the myelin in juxtaparanodal regions
Nav channels at nodes of Ranvier; Kv channels in juxtaparanodal internodal membrane

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: What is the 'safety factor' for action potential propagation in a healthy myelinated nerve fiber?
options: The ratio of axon diameter to myelin thickness (g-ratio = 1.0)
The ratio of the local axial depolarizing current generated at an active node to the minimum current required to depolarize the next node to threshold (typically 5 to 7 in healthy myelinated axons)
The number of Schwann cells in the brain
The resting voltage of the astrocyte membrane
questions.explain: A high safety factor (~5-7) ensures reliable signal transmission even during high-frequency firing, mild cooling, or metabolic stress; demyelination erodes the safety factor below 1.0, causing conduction failure.

open.q: Define the safety factor for nerve impulse propagation.
accept: Ratio of local current generated by an active membrane region to the minimum threshold current needed to excite the adjacent downstream region (normally ~5-7)
Available depolarizing current divided by threshold current required at the next node

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: If an axon is stimulated electrically in the middle of its shaft (mid-axon stimulation), in which direction(s) do action potentials propagate?
options: Orthodromically toward the axon terminal only
Antidromically toward the soma only
Bidirectionally—both orthodromically toward the axon terminals and antidromically toward the cell body—because unexcited membrane on both sides is non-refractory
Neither direction; mid-axon stimulation never triggers a spike
questions.explain: Normally, spikes originate at the axon hillock and travel orthodromically because upstream membrane is refractory; artificial mid-axon depolarization excites non-refractory membrane on both sides, producing both orthodromic and antidromic spikes.

open.q: Contrast orthodromic and antidromic conduction, and explain why artificial mid-axon electrical stimulation generates both.
accept: Orthodromic travels from soma to axon terminal; antidromic travels from terminal toward soma. Mid-axon stimulation depolarizes non-refractory membrane in both directions
Orthodromic = normal forward conduction; antidromic = backward conduction; both occur because resting membrane on either side of a mid-axon stimulus is excitable

questions.q: In the Lloyd-Hunt numerical classification used specifically for sensory (afferent) nerve fibers, which fibers correspond to primary muscle spindle annulospiral endings and Golgi tendon organs?
options: Group IV unmyelinated fibers
Group III thinly myelinated fibers
Group II medium myelinated fibers
Group Ia (muscle spindle primary endings) and Group Ib (Golgi tendon organs), both equivalent to A-alpha fibers
questions.explain: Lloyd afferent groups map directly to Erlanger-Gasser classes: Group Ia/Ib = A-alpha (proprioceptors), Group II = A-beta (cutaneous mechanoreceptors, secondary spindle endings), Group III = A-delta (fast pain/cold), and Group IV = C (slow pain/warmth).

open.q: Match Lloyd sensory afferent Groups Ia, Ib, II, III, and IV to their corresponding Erlanger-Gasser fiber letter designations.
accept: Ia and Ib = A-alpha; II = A-beta; III = A-delta; IV = C
Group I = A-alpha, Group II = A-beta, Group III = A-delta, Group IV = C

questions.q: Which nerve fiber types carry preganglionic autonomic fibers versus postganglionic sympathetic fibers?
options: Preganglionic autonomic fibers are thinly myelinated Type B fibers (3-15 m/s); postganglionic autonomic fibers are unmyelinated Type C fibers (0.5-2 m/s)
Preganglionic fibers are A-alpha; postganglionic fibers are A-beta
Both preganglionic and postganglionic fibers are heavily myelinated A-alpha fibers
Preganglionic fibers are Type C; postganglionic fibers are Type B
questions.explain: Type B fibers are small myelinated preganglionic autonomic axons, while postganglionic autonomic fibers (except rare myelinated ciliary ganglion fibers) are unmyelinated C fibers.

open.q: Identify the Erlanger-Gasser fiber classes for preganglionic autonomic axons and postganglionic autonomic axons.
accept: Preganglionic: Type B (thinly myelinated); Postganglionic: Type C (unmyelinated)
B fibers preganglionic, C fibers postganglionic

questions.q: What is a 'triad' in mammalian skeletal muscle, and where is it located relative to the sarcomere bands?
options: Two T-tubules flanking one Z-disc, located at the M-line
One central transverse (T) tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, located at the junction of the A band and I band (two triads per sarcomere)
Three mitochondria surrounding a nucleus
Three myosin heads bound to one troponin molecule
questions.explain: Mammalian skeletal muscle has two triads per sarcomere positioned at the A-I junctions (whereas cardiac muscle has diads—one T-tubule + one SR cisterna—located at the Z-lines).

open.q: Describe the structural components and sarcomeric location of a triad in mammalian skeletal muscle.
accept: One T-tubule flanked by two SR terminal cisternae, located at the A-I band junction
Two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum plus one central T-tubule at the A-I junction

questions.q: What is the structural and functional role of dystrophin in skeletal muscle fibers?
options: It hydrolyzes ATP to generate the myosin power stroke
It pumps calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum

It links intracellular F-actin cytoskeleton to the sarcolemmal dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex and extracellular matrix, stabilizing the sarcolemma against mechanical shear stress during contraction
It synthesizes acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
questions.explain: Absent or truncated dystrophin (Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy) leaves the sarcolemma fragile during contraction, leading to membrane tearing, Ca2+ influx, fiber necrosis, elevated serum creatine kinase, and fibrofatty replacement.

open.q: State the structural role of dystrophin in skeletal muscle and the X-linked disease caused by its complete absence.
accept: Links intracellular actin cytoskeleton to sarcolemmal glycoproteins/extracellular matrix to stabilize the membrane; absence causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Anchors F-actin to the sarcolemma; Duchenne muscular dystrophy

questions.q: Which protein forms the central structural line (M-line) in the middle of the H zone that cross-links adjacent thick myosin filaments?
options: Alpha-actinin
Tropomyosin
Calmodulin
Myomesin (and M-protein)
questions.explain: Myomesin anchors thick myosin filaments at the M-line in the center of the sarcomere, whereas alpha-actinin cross-links thin actin filaments at the Z-disc.

open.q: Name the structural proteins that anchor filaments at the M-line and at the Z-disc of a sarcomere.
accept: Myomesin at the M-line and alpha-actinin at the Z-disc
M-line: myomesin; Z-disc: alpha-actinin

questions.q: What is the difference between an isometric contraction, a concentric isotonic contraction, and an eccentric isotonic contraction?
options: Isometric: muscle develops tension without changing length; Concentric: muscle shortens while overcoming a load; Eccentric: muscle lengthens while actively developing tension against a heavier load
Isometric: muscle shortens at zero load; Concentric: muscle never develops tension; Eccentric: occurs only in cardiac muscle
Isometric: ATP is not used; Concentric: Ca2+ is not required; Eccentric: actin is absent
All three contractions involve identical changes in sarcomere length
questions.explain: Holding a heavy weight steady is isometric; lifting it upward is concentric; slowly lowering it against gravity is eccentric (which generates the highest absolute force per fiber and causes the most delayed-onset muscle soreness).

open.q: Contrast isometric, concentric, and eccentric muscle contractions in terms of muscle tension and overall muscle length.
accept: Isometric: tension increases with no change in length; Concentric: muscle shortens under load; Eccentric: muscle lengthens while generating active tension
Isometric = constant length; concentric = shortening; eccentric = active lengthening

questions.q: Even during a purely 'isometric' contraction where overall muscle-tendon length does not change, why do the contractile elements (sarcomeres) still shorten slightly?
options: Because bones bend inward during every contraction
Because shortening of the contractile component stretches the series elastic component (tendons, titin, cross-bridges) to transmit tension to the bony attachments
Because the Z-discs dissolve temporarily
Because extracellular fluid enters the sarcomere
questions.explain: According to Hill's three-element muscle model (contractile component + series elastic component + parallel elastic component), internal sarcomere shortening stretches the series elastic elements before external force is registered.

open.q: Using Hill's mechanical model of muscle, explain how internal sarcomere shortening occurs during an external isometric contraction.
accept: Contractile elements shorten and stretch the series elastic elements (tendons and elastic proteins) while total muscle-tendon length stays constant
Sarcomeres shorten to stretch the series elastic component

questions.q: Which three metabolic pathways regenerate ATP in active skeletal muscle, listed in chronological order from immediate (0-10 seconds) to prolonged (>2 minutes) exercise?
options: Aerobic oxidative phosphorylation -> anaerobic glycolysis -> phosphocreatine system
Anaerobic glycolysis -> beta-oxidation -> creatine kinase
Phosphocreatine (creatine kinase) system -> anaerobic glycolysis (glycogen-lactic acid system) -> aerobic oxidative phosphorylation
Ketone body oxidation -> urea cycle -> pentose phosphate pathway
questions.explain: Stored ATP (~2 s) is immediately buffered by phosphocreatine via creatine kinase (~8-10 s), followed by rapid anaerobic glycolysis (~30-90 s), and sustained aerobic oxidation of carbohydrates and fatty acids for prolonged activity.

open.q: List the three energy systems that replenish ATP in skeletal muscle in order from fastest/shortest-lasting to slowest/longest-lasting.
accept: Phosphocreatine (creatine kinase) system, anaerobic glycolysis, and aerobic oxidative phosphorylation
1) Phosphocreatine, 2) Anaerobic glycolysis, 3) Aerobic oxidation

questions.q: What is the primary physiological cause of peripheral skeletal muscle fatigue during intense high-frequency exercise?
options: Complete depletion of intracellular ATP to zero
Destruction of all motor end-plates in the muscle
Permanent loss of myosin heavy chains

Accumulation of inorganic phosphate (Pi), H+ ions, and extracellular K+ (impairing T-tubule excitability, SR Ca2+ release, and cross-bridge sensitivity to Ca2+) combined with muscle glycogen depletion
questions.explain: Cellular ATP rarely falls below 60-70% of resting levels even at exhaustion (preventing rigor); instead, elevated Pi, H+, reactive oxygen species, interstitial K+ accumulation, and glycogen depletion impair excitation-contraction coupling.

open.q: Name three intracellular or interstitial metabolic factors responsible for peripheral skeletal muscle fatigue during intense exertion.
accept: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation, H+ (acidosis), interstitial K+ buildup, and glycogen depletion
Elevated Pi, H+, extracellular K+, and depleted muscle glycogen

questions.q: What is excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC, formerly termed 'oxygen debt')?
options: Elevated oxygen uptake after exercise ceases, used to replenish muscle myoglobin O2 and phosphocreatine stores, clear/convert lactate via the Cori cycle, and support elevated post-exercise body temperature and catecholamines
Complete cessation of pulmonary ventilation for 10 minutes after sprinting
Excretion of molecular oxygen in the urine after marathon running
A permanent drop in resting basal metabolic rate after training
questions.explain: EPOC consists of a fast alactacid component (resynthesizing ATP/phosphocreatine and reloading myoglobin/hemoglobin within minutes) and a slow component (hepatic gluconeogenesis from lactate, elevated temperature, and sympathetic hormone clearance).

open.q: List three physiological processes accounted for by excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC).
accept: Resynthesis of phosphocreatine/ATP, reoxygenation of myoglobin, and lactate clearance/Cori cycle gluconeogenesis
Replenishing ATP/PCr stores, reloading myoglobin O2, and metabolizing lactate

questions.q: Which structures in smooth muscle serve as functional equivalents to the Z-discs of striated muscle by anchoring thin actin filaments?
options: Intercalated discs
Dense bodies (cytoplasmic and sarcolemmal attachment plaques containing alpha-actinin)
Nodes of Ranvier
Triads
questions.explain: Smooth muscle lacks Z-discs and sarcomeres; instead, actin filaments attach to alpha-actinin-rich dense bodies in the cytoplasm and dense bands along the plasma membrane, causing the spindle-shaped cell to corkscrew/shorten when myosin pulls.

open.q: Name the alpha-actinin-containing structures in smooth muscle that anchor thin actin filaments in place of Z-discs.
accept: Dense bodies
Dense bodies and membrane dense bands

questions.q: What are caveolae in smooth muscle cells, and what functional role do they play?
options: Deep T-tubules forming triads with Z-discs
Small flask-shaped invaginations of the sarcolemma (analogous to rudimentary T-tubules) that cluster ion channels, GPCRs, and Ca2+ signaling microdomains near peripheral sarcoplasmic reticulum
Nuclear pores that export myosin mRNA
Mitochondrial cristae that synthesize acetylcholine
questions.explain: Smooth muscle lacks T-tubules; instead, abundant caveolin-lined plasma membrane invaginations (caveolae) lie close to peripheral SR cisternae to coordinate Ca2+ entry and release.

open.q: What are caveolae in smooth muscle cells, and which striated muscle structure do they functionally replace?
accept: Flask-shaped plasma membrane invaginations involved in Ca2+ signaling; functionally analogous to transverse (T) tubules
Sarcolemmal invaginations replacing T-tubules

questions.q: By which two mechanisms do hormones and neurotransmitters elevate cytosolic Ca2+ to initiate smooth muscle contraction without necessarily firing a full action potential (pharmacomechanical coupling)?
options: Opening voltage-gated Na+ channels and activating SERCA
Inhibiting phospholipase C and lowering IP3
Extracellular Ca2+ influx through L-type voltage-gated or receptor-operated Ca2+ channels, plus Gq-phospholipase C generation of IP3 to release Ca2+ from sarcoplasmic reticulum IP3 receptors
Opening chloride leak channels to hyperpolarize the membrane
questions.explain: Smooth muscle uses both electromechanical coupling (depolarization opening L-type Cav1.2 channels) and pharmacomechanical coupling (agonists like norepinephrine/angiotensin II activating Gq -> PLC -> IP3 -> SR Ca2+ release at constant membrane potential).

open.q: Distinguish electromechanical coupling from pharmacomechanical coupling in smooth muscle contraction.
accept: Electromechanical coupling triggers Ca2+ influx via membrane depolarization opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; pharmacomechanical coupling releases SR Ca2+ via ligand-GPCR-IP3 signaling without membrane depolarization
Voltage-gated Ca2+ entry upon depolarization vs agonist-induced IP3-mediated Ca2+ release without voltage change

questions.q: What is the 'stress-relaxation' (plasticity) property of visceral smooth muscle (such as in the urinary bladder wall or gastric fundus)?
options: Permanent rupture of smooth muscle whenever stretched by 10%
Immediate tetanic spasm whenever volume increases
Loss of all gap junctions during filling

When stretched to a greater length, smooth muscle initially develops high passive/active tension that gradually returns back toward baseline over seconds to minutes, allowing hollow organs to store large volumes at low internal pressure
questions.explain: Reorganization of non-sarcomeric actin-myosin cross-bridges and dense-body attachments lets the urinary bladder and stomach accommodate large volume increases with minimal rise in intraluminal pressure.

open.q: Define the stress-relaxation (plasticity) phenomenon in visceral smooth muscle and give one organ where it is physiologically vital.
accept: Transient rise in tension upon stretch followed by gradual return toward baseline tension; vital in the urinary bladder or stomach
Accommodation to increased volume without sustained pressure rise, as in the urinary bladder

questions.q: How do beta-2 adrenergic agonists (such as albuterol in bronchial smooth muscle) and nitric oxide donors (such as nitroglycerin in vascular smooth muscle) cause smooth muscle relaxation?
options: Beta-2 agonists increase cAMP (activating PKA) and nitric oxide increases cGMP (activating PKG); both kinases inhibit MLCK, stimulate MLCP, and promote Ca2+ sequestration/hyperpolarization
Both open L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels to flood the cytoplasm with Ca2+
Both activate Rho-kinase to inhibit myosin light-chain phosphatase
Both release acetylcholine from parasympathetic varicosities
questions.explain: Cyclic nucleotide pathways (Gs-cAMP-PKA and NO-sGC-cGMP-PKG) relax smooth muscle by lowering cytosolic Ca2+, opening K+ channels, phosphorylating/inhibiting MLCK, and activating MLCP.

open.q: Identify the second messengers mediating smooth muscle relaxation by beta-2 adrenergic agonists and by nitric oxide.
accept: Beta-2 agonists: cyclic AMP (cAMP); Nitric oxide: cyclic GMP (cGMP)
cAMP for beta-2 stimulation and cGMP for nitric oxide
