questions.q: What are 'slow waves' (basic electrical rhythm) in gastrointestinal unitary smooth muscle, and which specialized pacemaker cells generate them?
options: All-or-none Na+ spikes generated by Schwann cells

Subthreshold undulating oscillations of resting membrane potential generated by interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs) that bring smooth muscle near threshold so superimposed Ca2+-mediated spikes trigger contraction
Hyperpolarizing IPSPs generated by skeletal motor neurons
Mechanical vibrations caused by blood flow in the aorta
questions.explain: Interstitial cells of Cajal act as electrical pacemakers in the gut wall, generating rhythmic slow waves (3/min in stomach, 12/min in duodenum) via cyclic SR Ca2+ release and Ca2+-activated Cl- channels; when excitatory input depolarizes the slow-wave crest above threshold, voltage-gated Ca2+ spikes fire.

open.q: Name the pacemaker cells that generate slow waves in gastrointestinal smooth muscle and identify the ion responsible for the superimposed spike potentials.
accept: Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs); calcium (Ca2+ influx through L-type Ca2+ channels)
ICCs; Ca2+

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: Why are action potentials in visceral smooth muscle and cardiac nodal tissue typically slower-rising and more prolonged than action potentials in large myelinated axons?
options: Because their Phase 0 depolarization upstroke is driven by slower voltage-gated L-type Ca2+ channels rather than fast voltage-gated Na+ channels
Because they lack lipid bilayers
Because their intracellular potassium concentration is zero
Because they conduct impulses via myelin sheaths
questions.explain: Smooth muscle and SA/AV nodal cells rely primarily on L-type Ca2+ channels for depolarization, giving slower upstrokes, slower conduction velocities, and direct Ca2+ entry to trigger contraction.

open.q: Which voltage-gated ion channel mediates the depolarizing upstroke of action potentials in smooth muscle and SA/AV nodal cells?
accept: Voltage-gated L-type calcium (Ca2+) channels
L-type Ca2+ channels

questions.q: What clinical bedside signs elicit latent neuromuscular hyperexcitability (tetany) in a patient with hypocalcemia?
options: Babinski sign and Kernig sign

Chvostek sign (ipsilateral facial muscle twitching upon tapping the facial nerve anterior to the ear) and Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm upon inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes)
Murphy sign and McBurney sign
Rinne test and Weber test
questions.explain: Hypocalcemia lowers the activation threshold of voltage-gated Na+ channels in peripheral nerves, so minor mechanical tapping (Chvostek) or mild cuff ischemia (Trousseau) provokes spontaneous nerve firing and muscle spasm.

open.q: Name and describe the two classic clinical signs used to demonstrate latent tetany in hypocalcemia.
accept: Chvostek sign (facial twitching on tapping CN VII) and Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure)
Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign

questions.q: How does severe hypercalcemia affect neuronal and cardiac membrane excitability?
options: It triggers violent generalized tonic-clonic tetany
It shifts the Na+ channel activation threshold closer to resting potential

Excess extracellular Ca2+ increases external surface charge screening, shifting Na+ channel threshold to a less negative voltage (farther from RMP) and depressing neuromuscular excitability (muscle weakness, lethargy, constipation)
It lowers resting membrane potential to -140 mV
questions.explain: Hypercalcemia stabilizes voltage-gated Na+ channels so a larger depolarization is required to reach threshold, producing hypoexcitability ('groans, moans, bones, stones, and psychiatric overtones').

open.q: Explain how hypercalcemia reduces neuromuscular excitability.
accept: Excess extracellular Ca2+ increases negative membrane surface charge screening, shifting Na+ channel activation threshold farther from resting membrane potential
Hypercalcemia raises firing threshold (makes it less negative), requiring greater depolarization to excite nerves and muscles

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: What is the 'chord conductance equation' for calculating resting membrane potential when multiple ions are permeable?
options: Vm = (gK/g_total)*EK + (gNa/g_total)*ENa + (gCl/g_total)*ECl (a conductance-weighted average of each ion's Nernst equilibrium potential)
Vm = EK + ENa + ECl
Vm = gK * gNa * gCl
Vm = (EK - ENa) / 2
questions.explain: The chord conductance equation expresses Vm as the weighted average of each permeant ion's equilibrium potential proportional to its fractional membrane conductance (g_ion / g_total); if gNa increases dramatically during Phase 0, Vm moves toward ENa.

open.q: Write the chord conductance equation relating membrane potential (Vm) to individual ionic conductances (gK, gNa, gCl) and equilibrium potentials (EK, ENa, ECl).
accept: Vm = (gK/g_total)*EK + (gNa/g_total)*ENa + (gCl/g_total)*ECl
Conductance-weighted sum of EK, ENa, and ECl divided by total conductance

questions.sub: Resting Membrane Potential and Ionic Basis
questions.q: In most mature central nervous system neurons, how is the intracellular Cl- concentration kept low (~5-10 mM) so that opening GABA-A Cl- channels produces hyperpolarizing inhibition (IPSP)?
options: By the K+/Cl- cotransporter KCC2 extruding Cl- out of the neuron using the outward K+ gradient
By the NKCC1 cotransporter pumping Cl- into the cell
By voltage-gated Na+ channels importing Cl-
Chloride is completely absent from cerebrospinal fluid
questions.explain: Mature CNS neurons upregulate KCC2 to extrude Cl-, setting ECl (~-75 to -80 mV) slightly more negative than RMP (~-70 mV); in immature embryonic neurons, NKCC1 predominates, making ECl more positive so GABA is transiently depolarizing.

open.q: Name the neuronal cotransporter that extrudes Cl- in mature CNS neurons to keep ECl more negative than resting membrane potential.
accept: KCC2
K+/Cl- cotransporter 2

questions.q: What is the 'latent period' observed between an electrical stimulus applied to a motor nerve/muscle and the onset of measurable mechanical tension in a single muscle twitch?
options: The 2-to-5 millisecond delay required for action potential propagation along the sarcolemma/T-tubules, DHP-RyR1 signaling, Ca2+ release from the SR, Ca2+ binding to troponin C, and initial cross-bridge attachment
The 30-second period after death before rigor mortis begins
The time during which SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR
The absolute refractory period of the spinal cord
questions.explain: Excitation-contraction coupling steps precede actual cross-bridge force generation, creating a brief mechanical lag (latent period) after electrical depolarization.

open.q: List the physiological events occurring during the latent period of a skeletal muscle twitch.
accept: Action potential conduction into T-tubules, SR Ca2+ release via RyR1, Ca2+ binding to troponin C, tropomyosin shift, and initial cross-bridge cycling
Excitation-contraction coupling and Ca2+ release/binding prior to force generation

questions.q: What is 'treppe' (the staircase phenomenon) in skeletal muscle stimulated repeatedly at a low frequency that allows complete relaxation between twitches?
options: A progressive decrease in twitch tension due to ATP exhaustion
A progressive stepwise increase in peak twitch tension over the first several contractions, caused by incomplete Ca2+ reuptake between beats and warming of muscle enzymes
Complete failure of the neuromuscular junction
Conversion of Type I fibers into smooth muscle
questions.explain: Even when tension returns to baseline between stimuli, residual cytosolic Ca2+ and increased temperature/myosin light-chain phosphorylation slightly enhance force over the initial few twitches before a plateau is reached.

open.q: Define the treppe (staircase) phenomenon in skeletal muscle and state its primary ionic cause.
accept: Gradual increase in twitch tension during the first few repetitive stimuli despite complete relaxation between twitches, due to progressive rise in cytosolic Ca2+ availability
Stepwise rise in initial twitch amplitude caused by residual cytosolic Ca2+

questions.q: What is the optimal 'g-ratio' (ratio of inner axon diameter to total outer myelinated fiber diameter) in healthy mammalian myelinated axons that maximizes conduction velocity?
options: Approximately 0.60 to 0.70 (about 0.6 in PNS and ~0.77 in CNS)
0.05 (extremely thick myelin with almost zero axon lumen)
1.00 (no myelin sheath at all)
questions.explain: For a fixed outer fiber diameter, making myelin too thick shrinks inner axon radius (raising axial resistance ri), while making myelin too thin lowers membrane resistance rm and raises capacitance cm; optimal conduction occurs around g-ratio ~0.6-0.7.

open.q: Define the g-ratio of a myelinated axon and state its approximate optimal value in peripheral nerves.
accept: Ratio of inner axon diameter to outer myelinated fiber diameter; approximately 0.6 (0.6 to 0.7)
Inner axonal diameter divided by total fiber diameter; ~0.6

questions.q: Why do patients with multiple sclerosis (a CNS demyelinating disease) often experience transient worsening of neurological symptoms during a fever or hot shower (Uhthoff's phenomenon)?
options: Heat melts the phospholipid bilayer of unmyelinated dendrites

Elevated body temperature accelerates the inactivation rate of voltage-gated Na+ channels and increases K+ channel conductance, reducing the duration of nodal inward current below the safety factor needed to excite demyelinated internodes
Fever causes massive release of tetrodotoxin from astrocytes
Warm temperatures hyperpolarize all axons to -130 mV
questions.explain: At higher temperatures, Nav channels inactivate faster (shortening spike duration and total charge entry per node); in healthy axons the high safety factor (5-7) tolerates this, but in demyelinated axons with a safety factor near 1.0, warming precipitates reversible conduction block.

open.q: Explain the electrophysiological basis of Uhthoff's phenomenon (heat-induced worsening of conduction block in demyelinated axons).
accept: Higher temperature speeds Na+ channel inactivation and shortens action potential duration, dropping nodal depolarizing current below the reduced safety factor of demyelinated segments
Faster Nav inactivation at elevated temperature reduces charge transfer and causes conduction block in demyelinated fibers

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: What is a 'compound action potential' recorded extracellularly from a whole mixed peripheral nerve trunk (such as the sciatic nerve), and why does it appear graded with stimulus intensity unlike a single-axon spike?
options: Because single axons violate the all-or-none law inside whole nerves
Because extracellular electrodes measure synaptic vesicles directly

Because a whole nerve contains thousands of individual axons with different thresholds and conduction velocities; stronger stimuli recruit higher-threshold fibers (summating amplitudes) and separate into distinct A-alpha, A-beta, A-delta, and C peaks over distance
Because myelin amplifies voltage by 1,000 volts
questions.explain: Each individual axon still obeys the all-or-none law, but the extracellular sum of thousands of fibers grows smoothly from threshold to maximal stimulus (recruiting larger then smaller axons) and disperses temporally by conduction speed.

open.q: Why does an extracellular compound action potential recorded from a mixed peripheral nerve trunk show graded amplitude and multiple peaks?
accept: It represents the algebraic sum of action potentials from thousands of axons with varying recruitment thresholds and conduction velocities (A, B, and C fibers)
Recruitment of multiple axons with different thresholds and temporal dispersion of fast vs slow fiber groups

questions.sub: Action Potential Propagation and Cable Properties
questions.q: What are the three stages of Wallerian degeneration and axonal regeneration following complete transection (neurotmesis) of a peripheral myelinated nerve fiber?
options: Immediate fusion of cut ends within 5 minutes without degeneration

Distal axon and myelin fragment and are phagocytosed by macrophages/Schwann cells (Wallerian degeneration), proximal soma undergoes chromatolysis, and Schwann cells form bands of Bungner to guide proximal axonal sprouts at ~1-3 mm/day
Oligodendrocytes migrate into the limb to replace Schwann cells
Retrograde degeneration destroys the entire cerebral cortex within 24 hours
questions.explain: Unlike CNS axons (where oligodendrocyte myelin inhibitors like Nogo-A and glial scars block regrowth), peripheral Schwann cells clear debris, secrete neurotrophins (NGF, BDNF), and form longitudinal tubes (bands of Bungner) guiding regeneration at ~1-4 mm/day.

open.q: Contrast axonal regeneration capacity in the peripheral nervous system versus the central nervous system after axonal transection.
accept: PNS axons regenerate (~1-3 mm/day) guided by Schwann cell bands of Bungner and neurotrophic factors, whereas CNS regeneration is blocked by oligodendrocyte myelin inhibitory proteins (e.g., Nogo) and astroglial scarring
PNS regenerates via Schwann cells; CNS fails due to inhibitory myelin molecules and glial scar

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: How do 'voltage-clamp' experiments (developed by Cole, Hodgkin, and Huxley) allow electrophysiologists to measure individual transmembrane ionic currents (INa and IK)?
options: By freezing the axon in liquid nitrogen
By clamping the membrane potential at a fixed command voltage via a feedback amplifier so capacitive current (Cm * dV/dt) drops to zero and measured feedback current equals pure ionic current
By removing all lipids from the cell membrane
By injecting potassium directly into the nucleus
questions.explain: Because total membrane current I_m = I_ionic + Cm*(dV/dt), holding dV/dt = 0 eliminates capacitive current, enabling direct measurement of voltage- and time-dependent Na+ and K+ conductances.

open.q: Explain the biophysical principle behind the voltage-clamp technique used by Hodgkin and Huxley.
accept: Holding membrane voltage constant (dV/dt = 0) eliminates capacitive current so the feedback current directly measures transmembrane ionic currents
Feedback amplifier fixes Vm to eliminate capacitive current and isolate voltage-gated ionic currents

questions.sub: Voltage-Gated Ion Channels and Action Potential Phases
questions.q: What is the 'patch-clamp' technique (developed by Neher and Sakmann), and what fundamental discovery did it enable?
options: Recording whole-brain EEG from the scalp
Measuring blood flow in single capillaries
Forming a high-resistance gigaohm seal with a glass micropipette onto a tiny membrane patch to record picoampere currents flowing through a single ion channel molecule in real time
Staining myelin sheaths with silver nitrate
questions.explain: Patch-clamping proved that macroscopic membrane currents are the statistical sum of discrete, stochastic all-or-none opening and closing transitions of individual protein ion channels.

open.q: What is the patch-clamp technique, and what did it demonstrate about ion channel behavior?
accept: Using a glass micropipette gigaohm seal to record currents through single ion channels, showing discrete all-or-none stochastic opening and closing events
Single-channel current recording demonstrating unitary stochastic channel gating

questions.sub: Motor Units, Summation, and Muscle Fiber Types
questions.q: When a fast-twitch motor nerve is surgically cross-innervated into a slow-twitch muscle (such as the soleus), how does the muscle adapt over time?
options: The muscle degenerates into fibrous scar tissue
The muscle becomes completely unresponsive to acetylcholine
No change occurs because muscle fiber type is permanently fixed before birth
The slow muscle acquires fast contractile kinetics, faster SERCA pumping, and fast myosin heavy-chain isoforms dictated by the firing pattern of its new motor neuron
questions.explain: Classic Buller-Eccles cross-innervation experiments proved that motor neuron firing frequency (tonic low-frequency 10-20 Hz vs phasic high-frequency bursts) controls intracellular Ca2+/calcineurin-NFAT signaling and myosin isoform gene expression.

open.q: What do cross-innervation experiments demonstrate about the determinant of skeletal muscle fiber phenotype (slow vs fast)?
accept: The firing pattern of the innervating alpha motor neuron determines the contractile speed, myosin isoform, and metabolic profile of the muscle fibers
Motor neuron impulse pattern controls muscle fiber type expression

questions.q: Why can smooth muscle generate substantial active tension across a much wider range of resting lengths (from 0.5x to 2.0x resting length) than skeletal muscle?
options: Smooth muscle lacks rigid Z-disc boundaries and possesses side-polar myosin filaments (with cross-bridges oriented along the entire shaft rather than a bare central zone), allowing actin filaments to slide much farther
Smooth muscle contains twice as many Z-discs per micrometer as skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle uses tubulin instead of actin and myosin
Smooth muscle does not require calcium for contraction
questions.explain: Side-polar myosin organization and flexible dense-body attachment allow hollow organs (uterus, bladder, gut) to contract forcefully even when markedly distended or collapsed.

open.q: Explain the structural basis that enables smooth muscle to shorten by up to 80% of its resting length and generate force over a wide length range.
accept: Absence of fixed Z-discs and presence of side-polar myosin filaments without a central bare zone allow continuous cross-bridge interaction over large length changes
Side-polar myosin arrangement and lack of rigid sarcomere Z-discs

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive ascending symmetric weakness starting in her feet and legs over 5 days, absent deep tendon reflexes, and mild distal paresthesias 2 weeks after a Campylobacter jejuni diarrheal illness. Nerve conduction studies show markedly slowed motor conduction velocities and prolonged F-wave latencies. Which pathophysiological process explains her paralysis?
options: Autoimmune destruction of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Acute inflammatory demyelination of peripheral nerves (Guillain-Barre syndrome), causing loss of saltatory conduction and conduction block
Excessive release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
Hyperkalemic hyperpolarization of skeletal muscle T-tubules
questions.explain: Molecular mimicry following C. jejuni infection triggers autoimmune attack against peripheral Schwann cell myelin (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy), stripping internodal insulation and blocking saltatory conduction.

open.q: Identify the underlying electrophysiological defect causing slowed nerve conduction velocity and weakness in Guillain-Barre syndrome.
accept: Immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves impairing saltatory conduction and causing conduction block
Peripheral nerve demyelination

questions.q: A 35-year-old man experiences episodic severe muscle stiffness and painful cramps immediately after brief exercise, during which his muscles fail to relax promptly (myotonia). Genetic testing reveals a gain-of-function mutation in the skeletal muscle voltage-gated Na+ channel (SCN4A / Nav1.4) that impairs fast inactivation. How does defective Nav1.4 inactivation cause myotonia?
options: Nav1.4 channels fail to open during Phase 0, causing complete flaccid paralysis
Impaired h-gate inactivation allows persistent inward Na+ leak after an action potential, causing repetitive self-sustaining sarcolemmal firing and delayed muscle relaxation
Mutation destroys SERCA pumps in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Mutation blocks acetylcholine release from alpha motor neurons
questions.explain: In paramyotonia congenita / potassium-aggravated myotonia, incomplete Nav1.4 inactivation generates persistent inward Na+ current that repeatedly re-excites the sarcolemma after voluntary contraction stops.

open.q: Explain how a mutation that slows or impairs inactivation of skeletal muscle voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav1.4) produces myotonia.
accept: Incomplete Na+ channel inactivation causes persistent inward Na+ current that triggers repetitive after-discharges and delayed muscle relaxation
Delayed h-gate closure permits repetitive sarcolemmal action potentials after contraction

questions.q: A 19-year-old man awakens with profound generalized flaccid muscle paralysis the morning after eating a large high-carbohydrate meal following intense exercise. Serum K+ is 2.1 mEq/L (hypokalemic periodic paralysis), and EMG shows electrical inexcitability of the sarcolemma. Why does severe hypokalemia paradoxically depolarize and inactivate skeletal muscle fibers in this channelopathy?
options: Low extracellular K+ activates Na+/K+-ATPase to hyperpolarize the fiber to -150 mV

Insulin-driven K+ uptake lowers extracellular K+, triggering paradoxical depolarization via leaky gating-pore currents or reduced inward-rectifier K+ conductance, which chronically inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels
Hypokalemia destroys all actin filaments within 1 hour
Hypokalemia causes massive acetylcholine release at the motor end-plate
questions.explain: In hypokalemic periodic paralysis (Cav1.1 or Nav1.4 voltage-sensor mutations), carbohydrate-induced insulin shifts K+ intracellularly; reduced inward-rectifier K+ current plus aberrant gating-pore leak locks the sarcolemma in a depolarized state (~-50 mV), inactivating Nav1.4 channels so action potentials cannot fire.

open.q: Why does sustained membrane depolarization (whether from severe hyperkalemia or paradoxical depolarization in periodic paralysis) cause flaccid muscle paralysis rather than continuous contraction?
accept: Sustained depolarization closes voltage-gated Na+ channel inactivation (h) gates and prevents them from resetting, rendering the sarcolemma inexcitable
Chronic depolarization inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels (accommodation/depolarization block)

questions.q: A 44-year-old man undergoes general anesthesia with inhaled halothane and intravenous succinylcholine and rapidly develops extreme muscle rigidity, hypercapnia, tachycardia, hyperkalemia, and a core temperature rising to 41.2 C (malignant hyperthermia). Mutation in which receptor causes this life-threatening syndrome, and what is the specific antidote?
options: Mutation in skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor (RyR1) causing uncontrolled SR Ca2+ release; treated with intravenous dantrolene (which binds RyR1 to inhibit SR Ca2+ release)
Mutation in nicotinic acetylcholine receptor; treated with atropine
Mutation in cardiac beta-1 receptor; treated with epinephrine
Mutation in aquaporin-2; treated with vasopressin
questions.explain: Triggering agents open defective RyR1 channels continuously, flooding myoplasm with Ca2+ and driving relentless cross-bridge cycling and SERCA ATP hydrolysis (generating massive heat, CO2, and rhabdomyolysis); dantrolene directly blocks RyR1.

open.q: Identify the mutated sarcoplasmic reticulum channel responsible for malignant hyperthermia and name the specific pharmacological agent used to treat it.
accept: Ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1); dantrolene
RyR1 Ca2+ release channel; dantrolene sodium

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with progressive proximal pelvic-girdle muscle weakness, Gowers' sign (using his hands to 'walk up' his thighs when standing from the floor), calf pseudohypertrophy, and a serum creatine kinase (CK) of 18,000 U/L. Which genetic and cellular defect underlies Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
options: Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
X-linked frameshift/nonsense mutation in the DMD gene causing complete absence of dystrophin, leading to sarcolemmal tearing, Ca2+ overload, and progressive myofiber necrosis
Gain-of-function mutation in voltage-gated K+ channels
Deficiency of hepatic glycogen phosphorylase
questions.explain: Without dystrophin to anchor F-actin to the sarcolemmal dystroglycan complex, mechanical contraction shears the plasma membrane, allowing unregulated extracellular Ca2+ entry that activates calpain proteases and destroys muscle fibers.

open.q: Explain the cellular sequence linking dystrophin deficiency to myofiber necrosis and elevated serum creatine kinase in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
accept: Loss of dystrophin destabilizes the sarcolemma during contraction, causing membrane tears, pathological Ca2+ influx, protease activation, and leakage of intracellular CK into blood
Sarcolemmal fragility leads to Ca2+ overload, muscle fiber necrosis, and CK release

questions.q: A 31-year-old woman presents with episodes of unilateral optic neuritis (painful blurred vision), internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and lower-limb spasticity separated in time and space. Brain MRI shows periventricular white matter plaques, and visual evoked potentials show markedly prolonged P100 latency. Which CNS cell type is targeted in multiple sclerosis?
options: Peripheral Schwann cells
Oligodendrocytes (causing CNS demyelination and slowed saltatory conduction)
Skeletal muscle satellite cells
Enteric interstitial cells of Cajal
questions.explain: T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of CNS oligodendrocytes strips myelin from optic nerve and white-matter tracts, slowing conduction velocity (prolonged VEP latency) and causing conduction block.

open.q: Which glial cell is destroyed in multiple sclerosis, and how does this affect visual evoked potential (VEP) latency?
accept: Oligodendrocytes; demyelination slows optic nerve conduction velocity, prolonging VEP latency
Oligodendrocytes; prolonged latency due to loss of saltatory conduction

questions.q: During emergency resuscitation of a patient with severe hyperkalemia (serum K+ 8.4 mEq/L) and wide sine-wave QRS complexes on ECG, intravenous calcium gluconate is administered immediately. How does intravenous Ca2+ stabilize the cardiac and neuromuscular membranes within minutes without changing serum K+ concentration?
options: Calcium excretes potassium into the urine within 30 seconds
Calcium binds directly to potassium ions in plasma to neutralize their charge

Calcium increases external membrane surface charge screening, shifting the threshold potential of voltage-gated Na+ channels to a less negative value and restoring the voltage difference between resting potential and threshold
Calcium inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase pump
questions.explain: Hyperkalemia depolarizes resting membrane potential closer to threshold; raising extracellular Ca2+ shifts threshold potential upward (less negative) in parallel, restoring membrane excitability until insulin/glucose or beta-2 agonists shift K+ intracellularly.

open.q: Explain the electrophysiological mechanism by which intravenous calcium gluconate protects excitable membranes during life-threatening hyperkalemia.
accept: Elevated extracellular Ca2+ shifts the threshold potential of voltage-gated Na+ channels to a less negative value, restoring the normal gap between depolarized resting potential and firing threshold
Raises threshold potential via membrane surface charge screening to restore excitability without altering serum K+
